executive_summary: The defining thread of the day is the accelerating erosion of established institutional frameworks — legal, geopolitical, and procedural — under pressure from concentrated executive power and great-power rivalry. The Trump administration's decision to require green card seekers to leave the United States to complete their applications abroad represents a deliberate dismantling of longstanding immigration procedure, affecting millions and signaling a broader willingness to rewrite the rules that have governed American civic life. This connects directly to Foreign Affairs' warnings about nuclear brinkmanship between China and the United States and the strategic vulnerability exposed at the Strait of Hormuz — both pointing to a world in which the post-WWII institutional order is being stress-tested simultaneously on domestic and international fronts. The Economist's defense of America's elites sits in direct tension with this moment, raising the question of whether any stabilizing establishment remains capable of checking these shifts. Together, today's content paints a portrait of a global system under acute strain, where the rules that once provided predictability — in immigration courts, in nuclear deterrence, in maritime chokepoints — are being rewritten faster than new norms can replace them.

items.headline: Knicks win their ninth straight playoff game
items.blurb: The New York Knicks are on fire. They've won nine playoff games in a row after last night's 109-93 victory over the Cleveland Cavaliers in Game 2 of the Eastern Conference finals.

items.headline: Jalen Brunson turned into much more of a facilitator
items.blurb: He only had nine points through the first three quarters on 4-of-12 shooting and 1-of-7 from deep. But he also had 11 assists and just one turnover in the first three quarters.

items.headline: Josh Hart being the hero in the third quarter
items.blurb: Six of those assists went to Josh Hart, who went from struggling to hit shots in the first half (12 points on 5-of-12 from the field and 2-of-7 from deep) to being the hero in the third quarter (12 points on 4-of-6 from the field and 3-of-3 from deep). The Cavs were determined to make Hart beat them, and he eventually was up for the challenge. He finished with a playoff career high of 26 points on 10-of-21 from the field and 5-of-11 from 3-point range.

items.headline: Cavaliers were adamant that they just missed shots
items.blurb: Following the game, the Cavs were adamant that they just missed shots. There might be something to that. They made 38.8 percent and were 9-of-35 from downtown (25.9 percent). A lot of these were pretty good looks, and the Cavs were 13th in the NBA in 3-point percentage and fifth in effective field-goal percentage.

With men's hoops coach Will Wade also back in Baton Rouge after being canned for NCAA stuff in 2022, much of the gang is back together.

newsletters.title: Anthropic’s Code with Claude showed off coding’s future—whether you like it or not

items.headline: Anthropic's Code with Claude showed off coding's future—whether you like it or not
items.blurb:
At Anthropic's developer event in London this week, Code with Claude, attendees were asked if they'd shipped code written entirely by Claude. Almost half the room raised their hands. Many admitted they hadn't even read the code before pushing it live.

As tools like Claude Code get better, more and more developers are happy to hand their work off to AI. Anthropic says it wants to push automation as far as it will go. But not everyone is convinced that's the right approach.

items.headline: The Enhanced Games fit right in with the rest of 2026's longevity vibes
items.blurb:
This Sunday, 42 athletes will gather in Las Vegas for the inaugural Enhanced Games, a controversial sporting competition that allows the use of performance-enhancing drugs. The goal? To "push the boundaries of human performance."

The event embodies a zeitgeist of peptide-crazed looksmaxxing, where consumers are encouraged to get thinner than ever, optimize for longevity, and have their "best baby." In 2026, if you're not enhancing, what are you even doing?

items.headline: Google I/O showed how the path for AI-driven science is shifting
items.blurb:
During Tuesday's Google I/O keynote, Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google DeepMind, proclaimed that we are "standing in the foothills of the singularity." But what struck me as I listened in the audience was the context in which he said those words.

The contrast reflects two directions for AI in science. One builds specialized systems like WeatherNext for specific problems. The other pushes toward agentic, LLM-based systems that could eventually execute cutting-edge research projects without human involvement.

The big scientific announcement at I/O was Gemini for Science, which leans further into this agent-driven future. It can still call on specialized systems, but Google appears to be transitioning away from them.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
Many leading AI researchers have turned their attention to a new kind of system that understands the physical environment: world models.
Backed by researchers at Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Meta's former chief AI scientist, Yann LeCun, the idea is gaining serious momentum. Could it change how AI understands reality?

MIT Technology Review editor in chief Mat Honan, senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven, and AI reporter Grace Huckins unpacked it all in an exclusive Roundtables discussion yesterday.

breaking_digest.narrative:
Thursday brought a series of significant developments in immigration and national security policy. The Trump administration announced that green card seekers must leave the United States to complete their applications from abroad, a major shift in longstanding immigration procedure that affects potentially millions of applicants currently in the country [1]. Separately, the criminal case against Kilmar Abrego Garcia — the Maryland man wrongly deported to El Salvador whose case became a flashpoint in the administration's immigration enforcement battles — was dismissed [2]. Earlier in the day, Tulsi Gabbard resigned as Director of National Intelligence, marking a notable departure from the top of the U.S. intelligence apparatus [3].

On the business front, fast-fashion giant Shein announced the acquisition of Everlane, a brand that built its identity on transparency and sustainability. The deal pairs two companies with starkly different reputations and raises immediate questions about Everlane's positioning under its new ownership [4].
